title:
The improvement
associations
items: A homeowners' club that controlled who could live on a block
Started in Hyde Park in 1908 with 350 members
58 bombings in Chicago between 1917 and 1921
head: Homeowners organized to keep Black families out
body: An improvement association was a homeowners' group formed to control who could live on particular blocks.

Attorney Francis Harper started the Hyde Park Improvement Protective Club in the fall of 1908. It had 350 members. Members agreed to blacklist realtors who sold to Black buyers and to buy houses back from Black owners.
Black doctors, teachers and business owners had lived in Hyde Park for about fifteen years. The club targeted them.
statlabel: bombings at the homes of Black families and at the offices of agents who sold to them, July 1917 to March 1921

title: Article 34
items: A rule in the national code of ethics for realtors
Adopted June 6, 1924
Racial language removed in 1950
head: The realtors' code banned selling to Black buyers
body: The National Association of Real Estate Boards adopted Article 34 on June 6, 1924. It said a realtor should never be instrumental in introducing into a neighborhood members of any race whose presence will clearly be detrimental to property values.
Member boards had to adopt the code. Agents could be disciplined. Boards that refused to enforce it could be expelled.
The Chicago Real Estate Board had voted in 1921 to expel members who sold to Black buyers on white blocks.
statlabel: years the rule stayed in the national code. The association apologized for it in 2020.

title:
Restrictive
covenants
items: A clause written into the property deed
Covered 38 of Chicago's 85 square miles of housing
Unenforceable after 1948, but never deleted
head: A clause in the deed barred Black buyers
body: A racial covenant was a restriction written into a property deed. It applied to later owners, so one campaign could restrict a block for decades.

The Chicago Real Estate Board distributed a model covenant in 1927, drafted by Nathan William MacChesney. It read: no part of said premises shall in any manner be used or occupied directly or indirectly by any negro or negroes. It exempted servants.
Shelley v. Kraemer made covenants unenforceable in 1948. The clauses were never removed from the documents.
statlabel: square miles of residential land south of North Avenue covered by covenants, on one estimate

title: Blockbusting
items: Speculators sold white owners on the fear of Black neighbors
Bought at about $12,000, resold at about $22,000
Started after covenants stopped being enforced in 1948
head: Speculators bought low from white owners and resold high to Black families
body: Blockbusting was the practice of turning white fear into profit.

Speculators called white homeowners in the evening and left flyers under doors, warning that Black families were moving in and values would fall. An owner would sell for about $12,000. The same house was resold to a Black family for about $22,000 on a contract, because redlining blocked ordinary mortgages.
The white seller got less than the house was worth. The Black buyer paid more than it was worth.
statlabel: the difference on a single house between what the speculator paid and what the Black buyer was charged

title:
Buying on
contract
items: An installment sale with no ownership until the last payment
One missed payment allowed eviction
Average markup of 84 percent
head: Buyers paid for years and held no title
body: A contract sale was an installment agreement. The buyer made a down payment and monthly payments but received no ownership interest until the final one.
One missed payment let the seller evict the family, keep every payment already made, and resell the house on another contract.
Duke researchers estimate that 75 to 95 percent of homes bought by Black families in Chicago in the 1950s and 1960s were sold this way.
statlabel: average markup over what the seller had paid for the same building

title: Redlining
items: Federal grades of green, blue, yellow and red, in 1939 and 1940
Three or four Black families could get a block graded hazardous
Hyde Park was graded yellow
head: The government graded neighborhoods by race
body: The Home Owners' Loan Corporation mapped Chicago in 1939 and 1940 and graded every neighborhood green, blue, yellow or red.

Local real estate agents and lenders filled in the surveys. Most of the Black Belt was graded red. Hyde Park was graded yellow, or definitely declining, partly because it bordered Black neighborhoods.
A red or yellow grade could block mortgages, home improvement loans and business loans for every property on a block.
statlabel: white-owned Chicago banks surveyed by realtor Dempsey Travis that would lend to a Black family buying in a white neighborhood

title: Urban renewal
items: Public money cleared the land and chose the developer
Approved November 7, 1958, the first large one in the country
34 units of public housing were built
head: The city cleared the land and picked who rebuilt
body: Urban renewal let public agencies declare an area blighted, clear it with public funds, and select the developer for the land.

The Hyde Park and Kenwood plan was approved on November 7, 1958. It was the first large federally supported urban renewal program in the country. The University of Chicago's South East Chicago Commission ran it.
Agencies spent about $40 million buying and clearing land, then sold it to developers for about $4 million.
statlabel: families displaced. The university opposed public housing inside the renewal area.
